implementation_notes: Go's claim primitive is LoadOrStore: it returns the existing value and loaded=true when the key was present, or stores the given value and returns loaded=false - that false is the claim, in one operation. A plain map with a sync.Mutex works identically; sync.Map suits read-mostly, write-once key sets. Either is per-process, so it protects one replica only; the database variant takes over as soon as duplicates can outlive the process or several pods share the queue. Sweep entries by stored timestamp, because neither map has a TTL.
pitfalls: LoadOrStore claims the key before the work is done: if processing fails permanently, the claim must be released or the retry is swallowed as a duplicate.
The in-process map is unbounded; sync.Map has no expiry, so a retention sweep over stored timestamps is mandatory.
Treating any database or store error as 'duplicate' is wrong: only a clean failed claim means duplicate, transient errors must return for redelivery.

variants.name: Database claim with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
variants.implementation_notes: The durable claim: a claim table with a UNIQUE key, where `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (PostgreSQL, or INSERT OR IGNORE on SQLite) plus Result.RowsAffected() == 1 from database/sql is the atomic check-and-claim, and the business write joins the same transaction. Choose it whenever redeliveries can outlive the process or competing consumers (several pods) share the queue; the affected-rows check is the only reliable duplicate signal.
pitfalls: RowsAffected() == 0 is only meaningful for the claim insert; check it before the business writes reuse the same transaction.
A failed INSERT for any other reason (constraint, connection) must not be read as 'already processed'.
variants.idiom_name: database/sql + unique index with ON CONFLICT
